questions.question: What is the main difference between a data class and a regular class in Kotlin?
options: Data classes automatically generate equals(), hashCode(), toString(), and copy()
Data classes are thread-safe by default
Data classes cannot have mutable properties
Data classes are faster at runtime due to compiler optimizations
questions.explanation: Data classes auto-generate structural equality and utility methods based on primary constructor properties. Thread safety and mutability are unrelated to the data class distinction.

questions.question: When would you use a sealed class (or sealed interface) instead of an enum class?
options: When you need better performance than enums
When you need a restricted hierarchy where subclasses can hold different data
When you want to avoid using the 'when' expression
When you need more than 256 constants
questions.explanation: Sealed classes allow each subclass to hold different state/data, unlike enums which are singletons. They're ideal for representing UI states like Loading, Success(data), Error(exception).

questions.question: How do Kotlin extension functions work under the hood?
options: They use reflection to inject methods at runtime
They modify the original class bytecode at compile time
They are compiled as static methods with the receiver as the first parameter
They create wrapper subclasses dynamically
questions.explanation: Extension functions are syntactic sugar — the compiler generates a static Java method where the receiver object becomes the first parameter. They cannot access private members of the extended class.

questions.question: Which scope function should you use for object configuration (setting multiple properties)?
options: run — it returns a different value from the block
let — it provides 'it' reference to the object
also — it's designed for side effects like logging
apply — it returns the receiver and uses 'this' context
questions.explanation: apply returns the receiver object and uses 'this' as context, making it ideal for configuring objects. let/also use 'it', and run returns the lambda result rather than the receiver.

questions.question: What is the key difference between lateinit and lazy initialization?
options: lateinit is for mutable vars initialized later; lazy is for val computed on first access
lateinit is thread-safe; lazy is not
lazy can be used with primitives; lateinit cannot
There is no difference — they are interchangeable
questions.explanation: lateinit is for var properties initialized after construction (throws if accessed before init). lazy computes the value on first access and caches it (thread-safe by default for val).

questions.question: What does the ? operator do in Kotlin's null safety system?
options: Forces a non-null assertion at runtime
Makes a type nullable, allowing it to hold null values
Catches NullPointerExceptions automatically
Converts null to a default value
questions.explanation: The ? suffix on a type (e.g., String?) declares it as nullable. Kotlin's type system then forces null checks before use, preventing NullPointerExceptions at compile time.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and === in Kotlin?
options: == only works on primitives; === works on objects
== checks referential equality; === checks structural equality
== checks structural equality (equals()); === checks referential equality
They are identical — === is just an alias
questions.explanation: == calls equals() for value comparison (structural). === checks if two references point to the exact same object in memory (referential).

questions.question: What is a companion object in Kotlin?
options: A thread-safe wrapper for lazy initialization
A second instance of the class that mirrors its state
A base class that all inner classes must extend
A singleton tied to a class that provides class-level members without static keyword
questions.explanation: Companion objects are singletons associated with a class. They can be accessed via ClassName.memberName, similar to Java's static methods, but are actual objects with full Kotlin capabilities.

questions.question: What does the 'by' keyword do in class delegation?
options: Delegates implementation of an interface to another class instance
Creates a new thread for the class
Makes the class abstract
Enables lazy initialization of properties
questions.explanation: The 'by' keyword in class headers delegates interface implementation to another object, promoting composition over inheritance. The delegating class automatically forwards interface calls.

questions.question: What is a higher-order function in Kotlin?
options: A function that takes other functions as parameters or returns a function
A function that runs on a higher thread priority
A function with more than two parameters
A function that accesses private class members
questions.explanation: Higher-order functions accept functions as parameters or return them. They're fundamental to functional programming patterns like map, filter, and fold.

questions.question: Why would you use the inline keyword on a function?
options: To make the function run faster on multiple threads
To avoid creating lambda objects by copying the function body to the call site
To allow the function to be overridden in subclasses
To make the function accessible from Java code
questions.explanation: inline copies the function body to the call site, eliminating lambda object allocation overhead. It's especially important for functions taking lambda parameters to avoid performance penalties.

questions.question: What are reified type parameters used for?
options: Converting any type to a String at runtime
Making generics perform better at compile time
Accessing generic type information at runtime in inline functions
Enabling reflection on sealed classes
questions.explanation: Reified types let you use the actual type argument at runtime (e.g., T::class.java). This is only possible in inline functions because the type is inlined at the call site.

questions.question: What is the difference between const val and regular val?
options: There is no difference — they are interchangeable
const val is mutable; val is immutable
const val uses less memory; val uses more
const val is a compile-time constant; val is initialized at runtime
questions.explanation: const val must be initialized with a primitive or string literal and is resolved at compile time (becomes a static final field). val is a runtime constant that can be initialized from any expression.

questions.question: What does the 'open' keyword do in Kotlin?
options: Allows a class to be inherited from (classes are final by default)
Makes a class abstract
Opens a class for extension functions
Makes all methods public
questions.explanation: In Kotlin, classes are final by default. The 'open' modifier allows inheritance. Abstract classes are implicitly open. Interface methods are open by default.

questions.question: When should you use a value class?
options: When you need a class that only holds constants
When wrapping a single type to get type safety without runtime object overhead
When you want to create immutable collections
When you need faster serialization
questions.explanation: Value classes wrap a single value for type safety (e.g., UserId wrapping String) but are inlined at runtime, avoiding the allocation overhead of a wrapper object.

questions.question: What is a function type in Kotlin?
options: A type alias for lambda expressions only
A class that must implement the Function interface
A type that represents a function signature with parameter and return types
A way to make functions generic
questions.explanation: Function types like (String, Int) -> Boolean specify parameter types and return type. They enable first-class functions, letting you pass functions as variables.

questions.question: What is the primary use case for sealed classes?
options: Defining constant values
Creating performance-optimized singletons
Implementing dependency injection
Representing restricted hierarchies like UI states or events
questions.explanation: Sealed classes restrict class hierarchies to a known set of subclasses, making them ideal for modeling UI states (Loading, Success, Error) with exhaustive when expressions.

questions.question: What is a key difference between sealed classes and enums?
options: Enums are singletons; sealed class subclasses can have multiple instances with different data
Enums support inheritance; sealed classes do not
Sealed classes are faster than enums
Enums can hold complex data; sealed classes cannot
questions.explanation: Enums allow only one instance per type with limited data. Sealed class subclasses can be data classes with multiple instances, each holding different state.

questions.question: What do delegated properties enable in Kotlin?
options: Faster property access through bytecode optimization
Custom get/set logic delegated to another class via the 'by' keyword
Automatic serialization of properties to JSON
Thread-local storage for each property
questions.explanation: Delegated properties (by lazy, by Delegates.observable, etc.) let you delegate property access logic to a helper class, enabling lazy init, observation, and validation patterns.

questions.question: What is the difference between List and MutableList in Kotlin?
options: List uses more memory; MutableList is optimized
List is read-only (immutable reference); MutableList allows add/remove operations
MutableList is thread-safe; List is not
They have identical performance characteristics
questions.explanation: List<T> only exposes read operations. MutableList<T> adds add, remove, and set. Both refer to the same underlying collection — List is just a read-only view.

questions.question: What does flatMap do compared to map?
options: flatMap preserves order; map does not
flatMap is faster than map for large collections
flatMap transforms each element to a collection then flattens; map transforms 1:1
flatMap can only be used on nullable types
questions.explanation: map transforms each element individually. flatMap transforms each element into a collection, then flattens all collections into a single result.

questions.question: What is the key difference between List and Sequence?
options: Sequence can only hold primitive types
Sequence is always faster than List
List is thread-safe; Sequence is not
List evaluates eagerly (all at once); Sequence evaluates lazily (on demand)
questions.explanation: List processes all transformations immediately. Sequence applies transformations one element at a time on demand, which can be more memory-efficient for large datasets with many operations.

questions.question: What is the difference between an object declaration and a companion object?
options: Object creates a standalone singleton; companion object is tied to a specific class
Companion objects are faster; objects are slower
Object can be generic; companion objects cannot
They are identical — companion is just syntax sugar
questions.explanation: An object declaration creates an independent singleton. A companion object is associated with a class and its members can be accessed via ClassName.member, like static members in Java.

questions.question: What does Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) share across platforms?
options: The entire UI layer including layouts
Business logic, data models, and networking code
Native platform APIs directly
Build configuration and CI/CD pipelines
questions.explanation: KMP shares business logic (networking, data, business rules) across Android, iOS, desktop, and web. UI remains platform-specific unless using Compose Multiplatform.

questions.question: How do expect/actual declarations work in Kotlin Multiplatform?
options: actual is optional — the compiler generates a default implementation
expect creates a copy of the function on each platform
expect declares an API in common code; actual provides platform-specific implementations
expect/actual only work for classes, not functions
questions.explanation: expect declares an API contract in commonMain. Each platform (androidMain, iosMain) provides an actual implementation. This lets you share interfaces while customizing platform-specific behavior.

questions.question: What is Recomposition in Jetpack Compose?
options: Re-executing the entire Activity lifecycle after a configuration change
Re-running a composable function when its inputs change to update the UI
Reinstantiating the composable from scratch each frame
Recomputing only the layout of a node without running any code
questions.explanation: Recomposition calls the composable function again whenever the state it reads changes, so the UI reflects the new values. Compose skips recomposing functions whose parameters haven't changed.

questions.question: What triggers Recomposition in Jetpack Compose?
options: Any change to the device theme
Recompiling the application code
Changing the value of a State object that a composable reads
Calling the composable function manually from a callback
questions.explanation: Recomposition is triggered when a snapshot state (like MutableState) that the composable reads is changed. Compose skips recomposing any functions that don't read the changed state.

questions.question: How can you prevent unnecessary recomposition?
options: Wrap every composable in a remember block
Restart the Activity on every state change
Use only immutable top-level values with no State
Hoist state so composables that don't read it aren't recomposed, and keep lambdas stable
questions.explanation: Keeping state reads as local as possible and passing stable lambdas/precomputed values limits recomposition scope. Compose also skips recomposing a function whose parameters are equal (unstable ones are checked more aggressively).

questions.question: What is the difference between remember and rememberSaveable?
options: rememberSaveable restores the value across configuration changes (like rotation) and process death
rememberSaveable is faster than remember
remember never keeps data after recomposition
They are the same; the names are aliases
questions.explanation: remember caches a value only for the duration of a composition; it's lost on Activity recreation. rememberSaveable stores it in the saved instance state Bundle so it survives configuration changes and process restoration.

questions.question: What is State Hoisting in Jetpack Compose?
options: Storing all state in a singleton object
Moving state up to a common parent so multiple composables can share and control it
Converting state to static variables
Removing state entirely from composables
questions.explanation: State hoisting moves state (and callbacks to change it) to a caller/parent so the child becomes stateless and reusable, and multiple children can share the same source of truth.

questions.question: What is the difference between mutableStateOf and StateFlow?
options: They are identical concepts
mutableStateOf is always async, StateFlow is synchronous
mutableStateOf is Compose's snapshot state; StateFlow is a Kotlin Flow used outside Compose or collected into composition
mutableStateOf can only hold primitives
questions.explanation: mutableStateOf is Compose's observable UI state. StateFlow is a Flow-based, cold/hot data container that Compose can collect via APIs like collectAsState, useful when the source is a ViewModel or a data layer that already emits Flows.

questions.question: What is derivedStateOf and when should you use it?
options: A coroutine scope for background work
A way to cache a value forever
A unit test assertion helper
A way to derive a new state by transforming other state, recomputed only when inputs change
questions.explanation: derivedStateOf computes a value from existing state and only recalculates when the inputs actually change. It's ideal for expensive derivations, e.g., showing 'X items selected' based on a large list.

questions.question: What is the difference between LaunchedEffect and DisposableEffect?
options: LaunchedEffect runs a coroutine tied to composition lifetime; DisposableEffect runs a block with an onDispose cleanup
DisposableEffect is only for animations
LaunchedEffect cannot be cancelled
They are interchangeable
questions.explanation: LaunchedEffect launches a coroutine in composition for side effects like network calls. DisposableEffect is for setup needing explicit cleanup (e.g., listeners, observers) and requires an onDispose block.

questions.question: What is SideEffect and when is it useful?
options: Runs exactly once before the first frame
Runs a callback after every successful recomposition to sync observables outside Compose
Blocks recomposition until it finishes
Creates a new coroutine scope
questions.explanation: SideEffect executes its block after each successfully committed recomposition. It's for publishing Compose state to non-Compose observers, like updating a ViewModel with the current UI state.

questions.question: What is CompositionLocal and how does it work?
options: A way to store values in the database
A way to implicitly pass values down the composition tree without threading them through parameters
A global mutable singleton readable anywhere
A replacement for ViewModel
questions.explanation: CompositionLocal provides values implicitly to composables in a subtree via CompositionLocalProvider. It's used for theming and commonly-scoped values, but overusing it hurts readability and recomposition performance.

questions.question: What is the difference between Column and LazyColumn?
options: Column supports scrolling automatically
LazyColumn can only contain text
Column composes all children eagerly; LazyColumn only composes visible items lazily for large lists
LazyColumn cannot be scrolled
questions.explanation: Column places all children in composition and layout at once, fine for small content. LazyColumn composes only what's visible, making it efficient for large or unbounded lists by reusing views.

questions.question: Why use the key parameter in LazyColumn?
options: To limit the number of items
To encrypt item content
To change the column background color
To give each item a stable identity so Compose preserves state across reordering
questions.explanation: Providing a stable key lets Compose associate the item's state (scroll position, remember values) with the data item, so on reorder or deletion the state follows the item instead of resetting or leaking.

questions.question: What is snapshotFlow?
options: Converts Compose snapshot state reads into a Flow that emits on changes
Takes a screenshot of the UI
Snapshots the database state
Mutates state manually
questions.explanation: snapshotFlow produces a Flow from the Compose state read inside its block, emitting the new value whenever the snapshot state changes. It bridges Compose state to Flow operators.

questions.question: How do you collect a Flow in Compose?
options: Using Thread.sleep in a while loop
Using collectAsState or collectAsStateWithLifecycle inside composable scope
Using a global variable
Flows cannot be observed in Compose
questions.explanation: Compose offers collectors such as collectAsState (simple) and collectAsStateWithLifecycle (lifecycle-aware, from androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose). Collecting a Flow from a ViewModel exposes its emissions as Compose state.

questions.question: What is collectAsStateWithLifecycle and why is it preferred?
options: It automatically caches in a database
It is faster than all other collectors
Collects a Flow respecting the composable's lifecycle, pausing when not in STARTED state to save resources
It converts Flow to a list
questions.explanation: collectAsStateWithLifecycle (lifecycle-runtime-compose) stops upstream collection when the composable leaves the STARTED lifecycle state, avoiding wasted work and potential leaks. This makes it the recommended collector for production apps.

questions.question: How does navigation work in Jetpack Compose?
options: Navigation is not supported in Compose
Using Android Intents for every screen
Using the BackStack of Fragments
Using the Navigation Compose library with a NavHost mapping routes to composable destinations
questions.explanation: Navigation Compose uses a NavController and NavHost where you declare routes/destinations as composables. You navigate via controller.navigate(route) and arguments are passed through routes or saved state.

questions.question: How do you pass arguments between screens in Navigation Compose?
options: Define arguments in the route (path patterns like /detail/{id}) and read them via NavBackStackEntry
With a shared global singleton object
By writing them to a file
Arguments cannot be passed between screens
questions.explanation: Destinations declare typed route arguments (e.g., /detail/{itemId}). NavBackStackEntry.arguments returns the passed values, which you read in the target composable. Avoid passing large objects; pass identifiers instead.

questions.question: How do you handle configuration changes (like rotation) in Compose?
options: By restarting the process
Compose recomposes automatically; use rememberSaveable for UI state and ViewModel for survived state
By freezing the UI during rotation
Configuration changes are ignored
questions.explanation: On a configuration change, the Activity is recreated and composition is discarded. rememberSaveable preserves UI state in the saved instance state Bundle, while a ViewModel survives recreation for business state — the recomposed UI restores automatically.

questions.question: What are @Stable and @Immutable annotations?
options: Way to make a class extend Activity
Runtime annotations that add animations
Compiler hints that let Compose skip recomposition when the annotated object's values don't change
They disable recomposition entirely
questions.explanation: @Immutable and @Stable mark types as having a stable identity/equality, helping the Compose compiler prove that unchanged parameters can be skipped during recomposition. They're performance annotations, not behavioral ones.

questions.question: How do you optimize performance in large Compose apps?
options: Store all state in one top-level MutableState
Rebuild the UI on every frame from scratch
Use lazy lists, stable state, derivedStateOf, and avoid recomposing large subtrees
Disable the Compose compiler
questions.explanation: Performance comes from reducing recomposition scope and cost: LazyColumn for lists, hoisting state, @Immutable/@Stable models, derivedStateOf for derived values, and Coil/Glide companions for efficient image loading.

questions.question: What is a Modifier, and why does modifier order matter?
options: Modifier replaces the need for layout
Modifier is only for styling text color
Modifier order never affects behavior
Modifier chains UI behavior/layout/decoration; order changes the order of application, so padding, clickable, and size behave differently
questions.explanation: A Modifier wraps/orders elements: e.g., Modifier.padding() applies padding to its content, and whether clickable or padding comes first changes what area is clickable and how it's laid out — so order genuinely matters.

questions.question: What is the difference between mutableStateOf and a plain val in Compose?
options: Changes to a MutableState trigger recomposition of readers; a plain val does not
A plain val also triggers recomposition when reassigned
mutableStateOf is slower in every case
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Assigning a new value to a MutableState marks the composition that reads it as dirty, causing recomposition. A plain val holds no snapshot state and does not notify Compose of changes, so the UI won't update.

questions.question: What problem does rememberUpdatedState solve?
options: Caches network responses
Keeps a long-running effect using the latest callback value without restarting the effect
Saves data to disk
Prevents all recomposition
questions.explanation: rememberUpdatedState lets a long-lived coroutine/effect (e.g., in LaunchedEffect) read the most recent value of a parameter without restarting when the parameter changes — useful for callbacks in animations or indefinite processes.

questions.question: How do you model one-shot events (navigation, snackbars) so they are not repeated on recomposition?
options: Store events in a persistent database
Replay the event on every recomposition
Consume the event once using Channels or one-shot event wrappers that are cleared after handling
Use a plain State that never clears
questions.explanation: Ui events sent as one-shot (e.g., through a Channel or a SharedFlow with replay=0, or a dedicated wrapper) are consumed by the UI once. If modeled as plain State/SharedFlow with old values, a recomposition or re-subscribe can re-trigger navigation or repeated snackbars.

questions.question: What are the main Coroutine Dispatchers in Android?
options: Main, Background, and UiThread dispatchers only
CPU, GPU, Network, and Disk dispatchers
Dispatchers.Main, Dispatchers.IO, Dispatchers.Default, and Dispatchers.Unconfined
Confinement, Parallel, and Serial dispatchers
questions.explanation: Dispatchers.Main runs on the UI thread, IO is for blocking I/O, Default for CPU-bound work, and Unconfined is not confined to a fixed thread. Choosing the right dispatcher controls where each block of work executes.

questions.question: What is the difference between viewModelScope and lifecycleScope?
options: They are the same scope
lifecycleScope survives process death
viewModelScope only supports Dispatchers.Main
viewModelScope is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared; lifecycleScope is cancelled when the Lifecycle is destroyed
questions.explanation: viewModelScope is tied to the ViewModel's onCleared(), while lifecycleScope (lifecycle-runtime-ktx) is tied to a LifecycleOwner and cancels on destroy. Pick the scope whose lifecycle matches the work's owner.

questions.question: What is a Coroutine and why is it better than Threads?
options: A lightweight concurrency primitive that suspends instead of blocking, allowing many of them on few threads
A special kind of CPU thread
A thread that always runs on the main thread
A replacement for OS processes
questions.explanation: Coroutines suspend rather than block, so a waiting coroutine frees its thread. This lets you run thousands of coroutines on a small thread pool and write sequential-looking async code.

questions.question: What is a Suspend Function?
options: A function that always blocks the calling thread
A function that can pause and resume on a thread without blocking it, callable only from a coroutine
A synchronous function declared final
A function that runs automatically in parallel
questions.explanation: A suspend function can suspend the coroutine (releasing the thread) and resume later. Suspend functions may only be called from a coroutine or another suspend function.

questions.question: What is the difference between launch and async?
options: async can only run on the main thread
launch is sequential and async is always parallel
launch returns a Job with no result; async returns a Deferred you await() for the value
launch returns a result and async returns a Job
questions.explanation: launch runs a fire-and-forget coroutine returning Job. async computes a value wrapped in Deferred, retrieved with await(), which suspends until the result is ready. Use async only when you need the result.

questions.question: What is Structured Concurrency?
options: Disallowing nested coroutines
Forcing every coroutine onto the same thread
Running each coroutine in its own process
Children share the parent scope's lifetime so cancellation or failure of the parent cancels the subtree
questions.explanation: Structured concurrency scopes children to their parent: the parent waits for children, and cancelling/failing the parent cancels all children, preventing leaks and orphaned work.

questions.question: What is the difference between coroutineScope and supervisorScope?
options: coroutineScope cancels siblings when a child fails; supervisorScope lets each child fail independently
supervisorScope always runs children in parallel
coroutineScope cannot launch children
They are interchangeable
questions.explanation: supervisorScope uses a SupervisorJob so one child's failure does not cancel siblings, useful in UI scopes. coroutineScope propagates failure and cancels the whole scope; use it when a failure should abort the group.

questions.question: What is the difference between Flow and LiveData?
options: Flow only works with Room
Flow is a cold stream with rich operators; LiveData is a lifecycle-aware value holder for the UI
LiveData supports backpressure internally
Flow automatically survives configuration changes
questions.explanation: Flow is cold — each collector starts the source — and offers transform/combine/catch and flowOn. LiveData is lifecycle-aware, caches one value, and is primarily a UI abstraction. In modern architecture Flow tends to be used at the data/domain layers.

questions.question: What is a cold Flow, and what is a hot Flow?
options: Cold flows are synchronous only
Cold always runs on IO; hot on Main
Cold: produced fresh for each collector; Hot: emits independently, collectors share the emissions
They refer to the flow's cache temperature
questions.explanation: A cold flow (e.g., flow {}) runs its producer for every new collector, replaying from the start. A hot flow (SharedFlow/StateFlow) has its own independent emission lifetime; late subscribers only see new (or replayed) values.

questions.question: Explain StateFlow and SharedFlow.
options: StateFlow is synchronous only
StateFlow emits every value and SharedFlow only the first
StateFlow holds one state and conflates to the latest; SharedFlow emits many events with configurable replay and buffer options
They are aliases
questions.explanation: StateFlow always has a value (data), merges concurrent updates to the latest, and is hot. SharedFlow supports many real-time events with a replay buffer and onBufferOverflow policy, making it suited for one-shot event streams.

questions.question: How do you handle thread safety in Coroutines?
options: Force every coroutine onto Dispatchers.Main
Rely on runBlocking to serialize everything
Never allow sharing state between coroutines
Restrict mutable state to a single thread/context or use atomic/thread-safe structures for cross-thread access
questions.explanation: Mutable state read/written from multiple dispatchers must be protected: confine it to one context, use Mutex/Actors/Channels for single-writer access, or use atomics and concurrent collections — matching the access pattern.

questions.question: What is Context Preservation in Flows?
options: The flow's collection context is preserved unless explicitly changed with flowOn or withContext
All flows must run on the main thread
The context changes automatically per emission
Flows have no execution context
questions.explanation: A flow builder runs in the collector's context by default. Operators like flowOn and withContext switch it, and each switch preserves the emission context, dictating which thread upstream work runs on.

questions.question: What does withContext do?
options: Spins up a coroutine that runs forever
Suspends the current coroutine, runs the block on the specified dispatcher, then resumes on the original one
Cancels the current scope
Blocks the thread without suspending
questions.explanation: withContext switches execution to another dispatcher (e.g., Dispatchers.IO) for the block, suspending rather than blocking, then restores the original dispatcher. It's the idiomatic way to do off-main work inside a suspend function.

questions.question: What is the difference between collect and collectLatest?
options: collect is deprecated
collectLatest is always dramatically faster
collect handles emissions in order; collectLatest cancels the current block when a new value arrives
collectLatest preserves order strictly
questions.explanation: collect processes each value to completion before the next. collectLatest cancels the ongoing collection block as soon as the next value arrives, dropping slow stale processing — ideal when only the newest value matters.

questions.question: How does CoroutineExceptionHandler work?
options: It prevents exceptions from ever propagating
It automatically fixes any exception
It only works inside runBlocking
It catches uncaught exceptions routed through the context, but is not used with SupervisorJob where each child handles its own failures
questions.explanation: A CoroutineExceptionHandler catches uncaught exceptions delivered to it via the coroutine context. With a SupervisorJob, each child has its own handler, and it never sees CancellationException.

questions.question: What is a concurrent map and when would you use it?
options: A thread-safe map (e.g., ConcurrentHashMap) for sharing key/value state across threads with fine-grained locking
A map that compresses its keys
A map used only inside Compose
A map that skips hashing entirely
questions.explanation: A concurrent map lets multiple threads safely access distinct keys without a single global lock, good for caches or state shared across coroutines/threads where a Mutex would serialize everything — at a small overhead cost.

questions.question: What are Coroutine Scopes and why are they important?
options: They optimize thread-pool sizes automatically
They define the lifetime and structured-concurrency rules of the coroutines they launch, preventing leaks
They replace the Android Lifecycle
They add runtime security permissions
questions.explanation: A scope ties its coroutines to a lifecycle; when the scope is cancelled (e.g., onCleared), all its jobs cancel. Component-lifecycle scopes like viewModelScope and lifecycleScope ensure background work never outlives its owner.

questions.question: What are the current recommended options for asynchronous work in Android?
options: RxJava as the sole standard
Raw Threads and Handler for everything
Kotlin Coroutines and Flow, plus WorkManager for guaranteed or expedited background work
AsyncTask
questions.explanation: The modern standard is Coroutines + Flow for composable concurrency and WorkManager for deferrable/guaranteed background jobs (e.g., sync, uploads). RxJava is legacy, and AsyncTask/raw threads are discouraged.

questions.question: Coroutines vs RxJava — which would you choose for a 2026 Android project?
options: Both are mandatory for a greenfield app
RxJava, because it has more operators
Raw threads, for the most control
Coroutines/Flow, as they are the native, lower-boilerplate, fully supported path forward
questions.explanation: Coroutines + Flow are first-class Kotlin, integrate with lifecycle scopes, avoid the reactive operator learning curve, and are Google-recommended. RxJava is heavier, legacy, and unnecessary for new projects.

questions.question: What is runBlocking, and when should you use it in Android?
options: It is identical to launch
It runs coroutines asynchronously without blocking
It must wrap every coroutine call
It blocks the calling thread to run coroutines to completion; use it in tests or main() bridging, never in UI code
questions.explanation: runBlocking blocks the current thread until its coroutines finish, fine for tests and top-level bridging but catastrophic on the UI/Main thread since it freezes rendering. Use suspend functions and scopes in production instead.

questions.question: If a parent coroutine is cancelled, what happens to its children?
options: All children are recursively cancelled
Children keep running independently
Only the first child is cancelled
Children restart automatically
questions.explanation: Under structured concurrency, cancelling a parent recursively cancels its entire job subtree. Each child receives cancellation and can run cooperative cleanup in finally/onCatch, guaranteeing no orphaned background work.

questions.question: Why favor Composition over Inheritance in Android?
options: Inheritance cannot express code reuse
Composition is always faster at runtime
Composition offers flexible, testable behavior by assembling objects, avoiding tight coupling to a rigid base hierarchy
Composition removes the need for interfaces
questions.explanation: Composition lets you build varied behavior by combining small pieces (interfaces + delegates), is easier to mock/test, and avoids deep, fragile class hierarchies. Inheritance is kept for clear is-a relationships where it's genuinely appropriate.

questions.question: What is the difference between MVVM and MVI?
options: MVI is the same as MVC
MVI has no ViewModel
MVVM requires RxJava
MVVM exposes separate state + events to the View; MVI treats UI state as immutable and drives it from explicit intents/actions
questions.explanation: In MVVM the ViewModel exposes StateFlow/LiveData plus separate one-shot events. In MVI the UI renders from a single immutable UiState and user actions become intents that the reducer folds into that state, making it easier to reason about.

questions.question: In a Clean Architecture, how do you distribute responsibilities between UI, ViewModel, Repository, and Use Cases?
options: Use Cases orchestrate domain logic; the Repository is the single source of data; the ViewModel maps domain state to UiState; the UI renders/collects
The ViewModel does all database work directly
Use Cases are replaced by the Repository
The UI talks directly to the database
questions.explanation: Clean Architecture layers dependencies inward: Use Cases (domain) define intent, the Repository (data) fetches/combines sources, the ViewModel maps results into UiState, and the UI only renders and forwards events — keeping each layer testable and swappable.

questions.question: How would you unit test a ViewModel that depends on an asynchronous Use Case using Mockito?
options: Call the real database in the test
Mock the Use Case's suspending result and drive the coroutine scope with a test dispatcher, then assert on emitted state
Run the ViewModel on the main thread without instrumentation
Assert only on the time the method takes
questions.explanation: You stub the Use Case to return a known result and control coroutine execution via a test dispatcher (and a rule for Dispatchers.Main). Then you observe the ViewModel's state/events and assert. No real I/O is needed.

questions.question: What concrete improvements would you apply to improve RecyclerView performance?
options: Load images synchronously on the main thread
Recreate the adapter on every scroll
setHasFixedSize, DiffUtil, stable IDs, enabling add/remove animations, and avoiding heavy binding work on every bind
Use findViewByid for each item in onBindViewHolder
questions.explanation: RecyclerView performance comes from stable IDs + DiffUtil to minimize changes, setHasFixedSize(true) to skip measurement, recycling via ViewHolders, and doing image/network work off-thread so binding is cheap.

questions.question: When does it make more sense to use Room, DataStore, or other caching strategies?
options: Always use Room even for one bool
Room for relational, queryable data; DataStore for simple key-value/preferences; in-memory or API caches for ephemeral data
DataStore for everything
Caching is never worth the complexity
questions.explanation: Room suits structured relational data with queries (entities, DAOs). DataStore (Preferences/Proto) fits small typed or key-value state. For short-lived UI or network data, in-memory or disk caches avoid premature persistence. Match the store to the data's shape and access pattern.

questions.question: How would you manage a bug that only occurs in production on a specific device?
options: Push a broad rewrite to fix it
Reproduce on an emulator blindly
Reproduce with the reported device/profile + logs, add targeted logging, and inspect crash analytics before changing the minimal code path
Ask users to reinstall the OS
questions.explanation: For device-specific production bugs you lean on crash analytics, logs, and device profiles, reproduce with the same conditions (Samsung-specific behavior, regional settings), add instrumentation, and isolate the smallest affected path before shipping a fix.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between modularized architecture and a monolith?
options: A monolith can never be tested
Modules always reduce build time with no cost
Modules give cleaner boundaries, better build caching and parallelization, but add overhead; a monolith is simpler but harder to scale sustainably
Modularization always increases binary size permanently
questions.explanation: Modularization improves separation of concerns and Gradle build caching, but adds complexity around inter-module APIs, ownership, and dependency graphs. A monolith is quicker to start and refactor within, but coupling grows. Choose based on team size and app scale.

questions.question: Explain the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) and why it matters for Android architecture.
options: DIP requires inheritance everywhere
Depend only on concrete classes
DIP means using only the highest-level layer
High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete low-level details, so implementations can be swapped/tested
questions.explanation: DIP says depend on abstractions (interfaces) rather than details, inverting the direction of dependency. In Android this lets you swap implementations (e.g., fake vs. real repository) and unit test without real I/O.

questions.question: Dependency Injection vs. Service Locator — what are the trade-offs?
options: DI is explicit and compile-time-safe but more boilerplate; Service Locator is simpler but hides dependencies and is harder to test
Service Locator is always compile-time safe
DI has no testing benefit
Service Locator can never be used with interfaces
questions.explanation: DI (e.g., Hilt/Dagger) supplies dependencies explicitly through constructors, making them visible and easily fakeable, at the cost of setup code. Service Locator is convenient and less verbose but centralizes discovery, obscuring dependencies and making tests rely on global state.

questions.question: What is Assisted Injection and when would you need it?
options: Injecting only string values
Injection where some runtime arguments (e.g., an ID) are passed at creation while the rest come from the graph, useful for factories
A way to disable dependency injection
Compile-time-only resource injection
questions.explanation: Assisted injection mixes DI-provided dependencies with runtime arguments needed per instance. It's used where objects require context-specific values (e.g., a repository built for a specific item ID) via generated factories, which Hilt/Dagger support.

questions.question: How would you design a scalable architecture for a multi-module Android app?
options: Circular dependency between all modules
Put everything in one giant module in a single layer
Layered modules (app/core/feature and shared data/domain) with clear interfaces and compile-time boundaries via dependency constraints
Never use interfaces across modules
questions.explanation: A scalable setup separates app (composition) from features and core, with shallow layers (presentation/domain/data) per feature, expresses modules via APIs, and defines explicit boundaries (avoiding circular deps) so teams can build and test modules independently, with feature discovery by navigation and dependency graphs 'inward only'.

questions.question: Describe the Android Activity lifecycle.
options: onCreate → onStart → onResume ... onPause ... onStop ... onDestroy, with onRestart between Stop and Start
onCreate → onPause → onStart → onResume
onStart → onCreate → onResume always
Activities only have onCreate
questions.explanation: The canonical flow is onCreate, onStart, onResume (visible/interactive), then onPause, onStop, and onDestroy (with onRestart between Stop and Start, and onSaveInstanceState before pause/stop). Each callback maps to the Activity's state.

questions.question: What happens during a configuration change such as screen rotation?
options: The Activity is kept forever
The Activity is destroyed and recreated, losing the instance unless state is preserved via ViewModel/SavedInstanceState
Only the layout inflates again, nothing else
The process is killed every time
questions.explanation: Rotation recreates the Activity: onSaveInstanceState captures transient UI state into a Bundle, onDestroy/onCreate run, and a ViewModel survives it. Compose recomposes with the new layout using saved/recall state.

questions.question: What is onSaveInstanceState used for?
options: To upload files to the cloud
To persist large user databases
To save transient UI state into a Bundle before the Activity may be destroyed, restoring it in onCreate
To cache network images
questions.explanation: onSaveInstanceState captures small, transient UI state (scroll position, entered text) into a Bundle before destruction. Restore it in onCreate or onRestoreInstanceState. It is not for large or permanent data — that belongs in persistence/ViewModel.

questions.question: What is a Memory Leak in Android?
options: Storing data on disk
An app that uses too much battery
A crash caused by a null pointer
Objects that outlive their lifecycle and hold references, preventing the GC from reclaiming them
questions.explanation: A leak occurs when a live object (e.g., an Activity/View) is strongly referenced after it should be able to be freed — such as via static references, anonymous inner classes, or long-lived scope closures — so the GC cannot collect it, slowly growing memory.

questions.question: Explain the difference between Serializable and Parcelable.
options: Parcelable is an Android-optimized protocol for efficient IPC/Intent transfer; Serializable is generic Java serialization that is slower
Serializable is faster than Parcelable
Parcelable cannot pass data
They behave identically
questions.explanation: Parcelable is designed for Android: writing fields into a Parcel is fast and lightweight, making it the standard for Binder/Intent IPC. Serializable uses reflection + full object graph serialization, which is slow, fragile, and risky for Android.

questions.question: What is a Fragment and why use it?
options: A background thread
A lifecycle-aware UI/behavior container hosted by an Activity, reusable across screens and back stacks
A way to store key-value pairs
A database table
questions.explanation: Fragments provide reusable UI and behavior with their own lifecycle within an Activity, aiding modular building blocks, back-stack navigation, and multi-pane layouts on larger screens. (Historically also used for configuration survival, now handled better by ViewModel.)

questions.question: What are Intent Filters?
options: Rules applied only to explicit Intents
A way to filter emails
Manifest-declared rules that match implicit Intents so the system can route them to a capable component
A permission checker
questions.explanation: In the manifest you declare intent filters with actions/categories/data that a component handles. The system matches implicit Intents against these filters to pick the target component, enabling deep links and component interoperability.

questions.question: How does RecyclerView improve upon ListView?
options: It replaces the need for adapters
It renders every item always, so there is no reuse
It can only show one item
ViewHolder recycling, adapter-driven layout with LayoutManagers, DiffUtil, and per-view access patterns
questions.explanation: RecyclerView decouples view creation/positioning, enforces ViewHolder recycling so widgets are reused instead of inflated, and pairs with LayoutManagers and DiffUtil for efficient updates. Progress/scroll responsibility are moved into adapters and item decorations.

questions.question: What is the difference between an explicit and an implicit Intent?
options: Implicit always targets a specific class
Explicit specifies a component class; implicit specifies an action and lets the system resolve a matching component
Explicit requires a broadcast receiver
They are the same
questions.explanation: Explicit Intents name the exact target component (e.g., startActivity(Intent(context, DetailActivity::class.java))). Implicit Intents describe an action/data, and the platform resolves which app/component can handle it (e.g., share or open a URL).

questions.question: Where does the app launcher label come from?
options: from a build-time environment variable
from the keystore alias
The android:label of the activity with MAIN/LAUNCHER intent filter, falling back to the application label/project name
randomly chosen by the OS
questions.explanation: The launcher reads the label on the launcher activity (the one with the MAIN + LAUNCHER intent filter). If absent, it falls back to the label on the <application> and finally the project/app name.

questions.question: How do components on the same screen communicate with each other?
options: Via hoisted state and callbacks in a common owner (ViewModel), or events/Flow between siblings
Through a direct reference to each other's views
Only via startActivity
By writing to a global static object (which is discouraged)
questions.explanation: Shared state that multiple components need is hoisted to a common owner (a parent composable or ViewModel) and propagated down as state; changes are communicated up via callbacks/events. Directly poking another component's views or random globals breaks data flow and testability.

questions.question: Background Service vs. Foreground Service vs. WorkManager vs. AlarmManager — when do you use each?
options: Use Background Service for everything
Foreground Service for user-visible ongoing work; WorkManager for deferrable/guaranteed jobs; AlarmManager for exact reminders; background services are limited by the system
AlarmManager for long downloads
WorkManager for real-time streaming
questions.explanation: Foreground services show a persistent notification for ongoing tasks (e.g., media/upload). WorkManager handles guaranteed, deferrable background work with constraints and retries. AlarmManager triggers exact/inexact alarms/reminders. Plain background services are restricted by background execution limits.

questions.question: What is a PendingIntent and why does it matter for security?
options: A way to skip the activity stack
An Intent that is never sent
A token that grants another component the permission to perform an Intent on your app later; if misused it can be exploited
A encrypted copy of the Intent
questions.explanation: A PendingIntent grants a third party (e.g., NotificationManager, AlarmManager) the authority to execute an Intent as your app at a later time. Because of that delegated permission, explicit intents, immutable FLAG updating, and unique request codes matter to avoid hijacking/mutation attacks.

questions.question: View Binding vs. Data Binding vs. Jetpack Compose — which and when?
options: View Binding for safe, simple findViewById; Data Binding to add binding expressions to layouts; Compose as the modern declarative UI default
Always use Data Binding no matter what
Compose is only for simple UIs
View Binding cannot be used for any modern app
questions.explanation: View Binding generates type-safe references without boilerplate. Data Binding additionally enables layout-binding expressions (and two-way binding) at the cost of build complexity. Jetpack Compose is the recommended declarative UI approach; the XML pair are recommended mostly for legacy maintenance.

questions.question: How do you choose between StateFlow and SharedFlow (and MutableList) for upcoming data and events?
options: Always use MutableList everywhere
StateFlow for single-value UI state; SharedFlow (with appropriate replay/buffer) for one-shot events; plain MutableList when state is local and not observed concurrently
SharedFlow for everything, including data
StateFlow cannot emit at all
questions.explanation: StateFlow is ideal to represent a single current value that the UI reflects (conflated). SharedFlow is a good fit for distinct events the UI must react to without missing them (choose replay and onBufferOverflow accordingly). Plain mutable collections suffice when nothing needs observing across scope.

questions.question: How would you implement analytics in a large-scale Android app?
options: Send events on the main thread synchronously
Call analytics directly from every View onClick
A thin tracking interface behind the app, fired from use-case/ViewModel events, with sampling, batched events, and no PII in logs
Log every keystroke to a file
questions.explanation: Analytics should sit behind a small interface (e.g., an AnalyticsTracker) injected and invoked from meaningful events, buffered/async, with stable event names and property schemas, privacy annotations, and no hard-blocking work on the main thread.

questions.question: How would you handle offline support and data synchronization?
options: Cache only the last screenshot
Load from the network every screen visit
Combine a local-first repository (Room) with a network worker, a sync policy, and conflict resolution (e.g., last-write-wins or versioning)
Ignore offline entirely
questions.explanation: Offline-first usually means the UI reads from a local Room cache immediately, the repository pulls updates from the network, Write-Ahead/queue for mutations, and WorkManager retries sync with dedup/conflict resolution and observable status so the UI reflects sync progress.

questions.question: How do you manage dependencies and versions in a modern Android build?
options: Use a version catalog (libs.versions.toml) to centralize, and pin reproducible versions with VCS-checked catalogs
Hardcode each version next to its import
Let each module pick any version it likes
Skip dependency management
questions.explanation: A Gradle version catalog in libs.versions.toml centralizes group/artifact/version, keeps builds reproducible and easy to update, and integrates with dependency locks and consistency checks across modules.

questions.question: What is R8 and how do you use it for shrinking, obfuscation, and keep rules?
options: R8 only obfuscates without shrinking
R8 adds new features to the app
R8 removes unused code/resources and obfuscates names; you define keep rules for code relied on via reflection or APIs
R8 is a database migration tool
questions.explanation: R8 runs at release build to strip unused classes/methods and shrink/obfuscate the app, boosting security and size. Keep rules (proguard/consumer rules for libraries) preserve code that must not be changed — e.g., reflection targets, serialization, DataStore, or the Gson models.

questions.question: How do you approach testing in Android?
options: Only UI tests, no unit tests
A test pyramid: many fast unit tests for logic, fewer instrumented/integration tests for UI and platform behavior
Only instrumented tests on real devices
Testing after every release only
questions.explanation: The pyramid favors many fast, cheap unit tests for business/domain logic, a middle layer of integration tests, and fewer UI/instrumented tests. This balances coverage and speed and keeps CI fast.

questions.question: What tools would you use to detect recompositions, and at compile time?
options: There is no way to detect recompositions
Only logcat string prints
Runtime: Layout Inspector / Compose surveyors; compile time: Compose compiler metrics and stability reports
Use the Garbage Collector logs
questions.explanation: At runtime, Layout Inspector and tooling shows recomposition counts; compile-time, the Compose compiler's metrics report functions/class stability so you can spot unstable params that prevent skipping and drive @Immutable/@Stable decisions.

questions.question: Have you used Hilt or Koin? Which would you choose and why?
options: Neither can be used in production
Koin is always the safest choice
Hilt never supports Android
Hilt for compile-time safety and Google support; Koin when a lightweight runtime DI with no kapt/ksp and simpler setup wins
questions.explanation: Hilt (Dagger-based) provides compile-time graph validation and scoped Android components, favored in large teams for correctness. Koin is a pragmatic runtime DI with less boilerplate and no codegen, chosen when startup/simplicity matters more than compile-time enforcement.

questions.question: What are some common performance pitfalls in Android?
options: Doing I/O or heavy work on the main thread, re-inflating views, over-recomposing large subtrees, memory leaks, and startup-time latency
Loading small images asynchronously
Re-inflating views without recycling
Calling Room to load data off the main thread
questions.explanation: Common pitfalls include main-thread I/O (ANRs/jank), wasteful view inflation or image loading, unnecessary Compose recomposition, leaks that grow memory, and heavy synchronous startup work. Fixes center on moving work off the main thread and reducing allocation/recomposition.

questions.question: How would you debug ANR (Application Not Responding) issues?
options: Reboot the device and hope it clears
Read the ANR's stack trace (/data/anr or logcat), identify blocking calls on the main thread, and remove or offload them
Increase the timeout arbitrarily
Ignore the trace and rewrite everything
questions.explanation: ANRs come from main-thread blocking (I/O, waits, heavy work) or stuck broadcasts. The ANR trace shows the main-thread stack; you pinpoint the blocking call, offload it (withContext(IO), WorkManager) or make it non-blocking, then verify no main-thread work blocks input for > a few seconds.

questions.question: JVM unit tests vs. instrumented tests — where do you draw the line?
options: Only JVM tests exist
Everything must be instrumented
Put pure logic in fast JVM tests; reserve instrumented tests for real Android framework/UI behavior that needs an emulator or device
Instrumented tests never require an emulator
questions.explanation: JVM (Robolectric/test) tests give fast feedback for business logic and state. Instrumented tests on a device validate real framework APIs/compose UI/parcelables/androidX where JVM fakes diverge — use them sparingly yet deliberately for platform-dependent behavior.

questions.question: What does a typical modern Android testing stack look like?
options: Instrumentation that only logs
Manual QA only
A single massive integration class
JUnit + Truth/AssertJ, MockK/Mockito, Turbine for Flow, Compose UI testing, Room in-memory, and Coil/network fakes for instrumented
questions.explanation: Modern teams combine JUnit/Kotlin test for unit tests, MockK or Mockito for stubbing, Turbine to assert Flow emissions, Compose UI + androidx test for UI, Robolectric for JVM android, and fake/architecture components (e.g., in-memory Room) for fast, deterministic tests.

questions.question: How do you monitor crashes and performance in production?
options: Crash reporting with symbolicated/mapping de-obfuscation, plus APM/RUM for latency/startup/ANRs/network metrics with thresholds and alerts
Check the app only at release time manually
Rely on the user reporting issues
No monitoring is needed if tests pass locally
questions.explanation: Production monitoring means automatic crash reporting (Firebase Crashlytics/others) with mapping uploaded so obfuscated traces de-symbolize, plus performance metrics (startup, ANR, frame pacing, network) and alerting so regressions surface before the users feel them.

questions.question: For live rates in a real-time app (e.g., currency exchange), HTTP Polling or Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
options: SSE only works offline
Always use HTTP polling for all rates
SSE for low-latency one-way server→client updates; HTTP polling when simple, low-frequency, or cost-sensitive data suffices
WebSockets are the only option
questions.explanation: SSE streams server→client updates efficiently for frequent, low-latency one-way data, reconnecting automatically. HTTP polling is simpler and acceptable for infrequent updates but wastes resources and adds latency at high frequencies. WebSockets are for full-duplex needs.

questions.question: How would you design a modular Android application?
options: Avoid interfaces between modules
Put all screens in a single giant module
Make every module fully depend on every other
Split into feature and core modules with explicit APIs, enforced boundaries, and shared navigation/DI, favoring compile-time safety
questions.explanation: Modularization groups code by feature and shared building blocks, gives each module a public API, maintains acyclic dependency rules, and centralizes navigation/DI. This improves build caching, parallel ownership, and testability at the cost of added coordination.

questions.question: How would you implement offline-first architecture?
options: Local cache as source of truth (Room), repository reads local and syncs via workers with conflict resolution and observable sync state
Block the app anytime there's no network
Store everything in SharedPreferences with no conflicts
Cache all images permanently with no invalidation
questions.explanation: Offline-first makes the local store the immediate source for the UI, the repository pulls from the network, mutations are queued, and a sync worker reconciles with the backend handling conflicts and exposing status — so the app is usable without connectivity.

questions.question: How do you implement feature flags in an Android app?
options: Hardcode if(true) everywhere
Remote config served per variant/experiment, cached locally, applied without restart, with kill-switches and analytics hooks
A value in strings.xml edited per release
Compile-time flags that require a release
questions.explanation: Feature flags come from a remote config with caching and defaults, support overrides per user/experiment, and can toggle behavior without a new build. They enable staged rollout, A/B experimentation, and rolling back risk quickly, tracked via analytics.

questions.question: How would you handle push notifications in a large-scale Android app?
options: Use one generic channel for every notification
Poll the server every second for updates
Firebase Cloud Messaging (or similar), with notification channels, tag/dedup, payload-driven navigation, high-priority for user-critical, and DND awareness
Ignore notification permissions entirely
questions.explanation: Layered approach: FCM to deliver messages, notification channels responsive to user prefs, dedup by tag/content, payloads controlling deep-link navigation, and data messages for silent syncing; foreground vs background handling differs.

questions.question: How do you implement app navigation with deep linking?
options: Deep linking is not possible on Android
Deep links require a separate app binary
Only HTTP links are supported
Map URIs/routes to destinations in the navigation graph, declare deep-link filters, and parse args to pass to the target screen
questions.explanation: Deep links (http/custom scheme) are registered as intent-filter data in the manifest and mapped to navigation graph args. On entry the system routes the URI, you parse the arguments (e.g., ids), and navigate, handling unknown/backup screens gracefully.

questions.question: How would you optimize app startup time?
options: Defer non-critical init, warm the startup screen lazily, minimize synchronous work in Application.onCreate, and profile with Baseline Profiles/Launch Latency
Do everything synchronously at launch
Start Network calls in the Application class
Instantiate all singletons up front
questions.explanation: Startup is sped up by deferring heavy init (DI, third-party SDKs) until needed, keeping Application.onCreate light, reducing cold-start class loading, using Baseline Profiles for JIT and Startup notices, and profiling launch latency with tooling.

questions.question: How would you handle app security, including data protection and certificate pinning?
options: Skip encryption to keep things simple
Encrypt data at rest and in transit (TLS + optional certificate pinning), enforce scoped storage/Keystore, validate inputs, and apply least-privilege permissions
Store tokens in plain SharedPreferences
Disable TLS verification in production
questions.explanation: Security defends in depth: strong TLS (with certificate pinning evaluated for its own risks), encrypted at-rest data via Keystore, minimal/least-privilege permissions, input validation, and never embedding secrets. Pinning sharpens MITM defense but must be managed carefully.

questions.question: What is Big O notation and why is it important?
options: It measures exact milliseconds of execution
It describes how an algorithm's runtime/space grows with input size, ignoring constants, to compare scalability
It is a type of sorting algorithm
It only applies to databases
questions.explanation: Big O gives the asymptotic upper bound of time/space growth as input size grows, dropping constants and lower-order terms. It lets you reason about how solutions scale before implementing — e.g., O(n²) vs O(n log n).

questions.question: What are Arrays and what are their time/space complexities?
options: O(1) for all operations
O(n) access by index
O(1) random access by index, O(n) search/worst insert/delete, contiguous memory of size n
No random access possible
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements contiguously, giving O(1) access by index. Searching an unsorted array is O(n); inserting/deleting in the middle is O(n) (shifting); the array uses O(n) space. Trade-offs with linked structures follow from contiguity.

questions.question: What is a Hash Table, and how are collisions handled?
options: It never needs a hash function
It stores keys in sorted order always
It allocates one slot per key only
It maps keys to buckets via a hash function; collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing
questions.explanation: A hash table applies a hash function to keys to index buckets, achieving O(1) average lookup. Collisions are managed via chaining (linked lists per bucket) or open addressing (probing), and good hash spread + resizing keep the load factor low.

questions.question: Singly linked list vs. doubly linked list — trade-offs?
options: Singly uses less memory and simpler traversal but can't go backward; doubly allows O(1) backward/predecessor access at a memory cost
Doubly always uses less memory
Singly lists cannot delete nodes
They are identical
questions.explanation: Singly linked lists store one pointer per node (less memory) and traverse forward only. Doubly linked lists add a prev pointer, enabling backward traversal and O(1) deletion given a node, at the cost of extra memory per node.

questions.question: Stacks vs. Queues — how are they different?
options: Stack is FIFO and queue is LIFO
Stack is LIFO (last-in-first-out); queue is FIFO (first-in-first-out)
They both use the same order
Queues only store numbers
questions.explanation: A stack pushes and pops from the same end (LIFO), used for undo, call stacks, and parentheses matching. A queue adds at the tail and removes at the head (FIFO), used for breadth-first search, buffers, and task scheduling.

questions.question: What is a Priority Queue and how is it different from a normal Queue?
options: It can only store integers
It has no order at all
It dequeues by priority (often max/min-heap) rather than arrival order
It is always sorted ascending
questions.explanation: A priority queue removes the highest (or lowest) priority element regardless of insertion time, typically backed by a binary heap with O(log n) insert/remove. A plain queue is FIFO regardless of priority.

questions.question: What are the different types of binary trees (full, perfect, complete)?
options: Perfect trees are unbalanced
Full and perfect mean the same
Complete trees cannot store data
Full: every node has 0 or 2 children; perfect: all internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves at same level; complete: all levels filled except possibly the last, filled left-to-right
questions.explanation: These classify structure: full (each node 0 or 2 children), perfect (full + all leaves on the same level), and complete (level-order filled except potentially the last, left-packed). Complete is what heaps require.

questions.question: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST) and what are its operations?
options: Each node is > all keys in its left subtree and < all in its right; search/insert/delete are O(log n) average and O(n) worst if unbalanced
BST guarantees O(log n) always
BST has no ordering of keys
BST only supports insertion
questions.explanation: A BST keeps the invariant left < node < right. Search, insert, and delete are O(log n) on a balanced tree but degrade to O(n) when it degenerates into a linked list (e.g., inserting sorted data).

questions.question: What are AVL and Red-Black trees, and how do they differ?
options: AVL is not a BST
Both are self-balancing BSTs; AVL is strictly more balanced (slower updates), Red-Black has looser balance with faster insert/delete
Red-Black trees cannot search
They store data unsorted
questions.explanation: AVL maintains a stricter height balance via rotations, giving better lookup but more rotations on writes. Red-Black balances less strictly (fewer rotations), making inserts/deletes faster with slightly taller trees — a common implementation for Maps/Sets.

questions.question: What is a Binary Heap and when would you use it?
options: A sorted array replacement only
A complete binary tree satisfying heap order (parent ≤ children for min-heap), used for priority queues with O(log n) insert/remove and O(1) peek
A tree with no ordering guarantee
A hash-table structure
questions.explanation: A binary heap is a complete tree where each parent is at least as small (min-heap) as its children, enabling an efficient priority queue: peek O(1), insert and extract-min/max O(log n), with no extra pointers using array indexing.

questions.question: What is a Trie (prefix tree) and when is it useful?
options: A hash table
A balanced BST for numbers
A tree storing strings by shared prefixes, enabling fast prefix search/autocomplete in O(key-length)
A sorting network
questions.explanation: A trie stores sequences by edges labelled with characters, sharing common prefixes. Lookups, prefix queries, and autocomplete are O(key length), making it ideal for dictionaries, IP routing, and typed-ahead suggestions.

questions.question: How do you represent a graph (adjacency matrix vs. list vs. edge list)?
options: All are identical in memory
Adjacency matrix is always denser than list
Edge list gives O(1) adjacency queries
Matrix: O(V²) dense/quick edge checks; list: O(V+E) sparse; edge list: compact list of edges with O(E) queries
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix uses V² booleans — great for dense graphs and fast edge checks. An adjacency list stores edges per vertex, ideal for sparse graphs and traversal in O(V+E). An edge list is a compact set of edges suited to Kruskal-style algorithms.

questions.question: BFS vs. DFS — when do you use each?
options: BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graphs and explores level-by-level with O(V+E); DFS explores deep via recursion/stack for connectivity, cycles, topological sort
BFS always finds the shortest weighted path
DFS is always faster
They produce identical exploration
questions.explanation: BFS explores breadth-first (queue/level order), giving shortest hops in unweighted graphs. DFS explores depth-first (recursion/stack), suited to reachability, cycle detection, and topological ordering. Choose by whether nearest-first (BFS) or deep exhaustive (DFS) matches the goal.

questions.question: Dijkstra vs. Bellman-Ford — how do you choose a shortest-path algorithm?
options: Dijkstra handles negative weights
Dijkstra is faster (O(E log V)) but fails on negative edges; Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and detects negative cycles at O(VE)
Bellman-Ford is always faster
Both can take zero-weight-only graphs
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy relaxation is O(E log V) but assumes non-negative weights. Bellman-Ford relaxes edges V-1 times, so it handles negative weights and can detect negative cycles, at the higher O(VE) cost — choose it for graphs that may contain negatives.

questions.question: Recursion vs. iteration — what are the trade-offs, and how do you avoid stack overflow?
options: Iteration can never be recursive
Recursion always uses constant stack
Recursion is elegant for divide-and-conquer but uses the call stack (risk of overflow); iteration is explicit and constant-space — use tail recursion or convert deep recursion to iteration
Stack overflow only happens in Java
questions.explanation: Recursion mirrors divide-and-conquer structures cleanly but each call consumes stack frames, risking overflow for deep recursion. Iteration avoids that but is more verbose. Techniques include tail recursion (if optimized), memoized recursion for DP, or rewriting deep recursion iteratively with an explicit stack.

questions.question: Compare the common sorting algorithms — which do you pick and why?
options: Radix sort works on arbitrary doubles
Bubble sort is always optimal
Merge sort is never stable
Quicksort/merge sort/heapsort are comparisons with O(n log n) typical; linear sorts (counting/radix) are O(n+k) for restricted inputs; choose by stability, in-place, and data shape
questions.explanation: Comparison sorts (merge, quicksort, heap) hit O(n log n); merge is stable and guaranteed O(n log n) using extra memory; quicksort is fast in place but worst-case O(n²); heapsort in place O(n log n) but unstable. Counting/radix sort hit O(n) for integer/limited keys. Pick by data and requirements (stability, in-place, worst-case).

questions.question: Linear search vs. binary search — when do you use each?
options: Binary search is O(log n) on sorted arrays; linear search is O(n) and needed when the array is unsorted or to find all matches
Binary search works on any array
Linear search is always faster
They are equivalent
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the range each step, giving O(log n) but requires a sorted structure with random access. Linear search scans each element O(n), used on unsorted data, linked lists, or when collecting every match.

questions.question: What is dynamic programming and memoization?
options: A way to write recursive programs that never cache
Solving problems by combining optimal subproblems and caching overlapping results (memoization) to avoid recomputation
Sorting in sublinear time
Looping without any state
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems with optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems, storing partial results in a table (bottom-up) or memoizing recursion (top-down) so each subproblem is computed once — reducing exponential brute force to polynomial.

questions.question: How should you secure a local Room database that holds sensitive user data?
options: Enable SQLCipher encryption and keep the key in the Android Keystore
Encrypt only the most sensitive columns and leave the rest plaintext
Rely on the app sandbox, since the OS already isolates the database file
Store the database on shared external storage so the filesystem encrypts it
questions.explanation: SQLCipher transparently encrypts the whole database file and the key is hardware-backed via the Android Keystore. Sandboxing alone does not protect against rooted devices or backups, and encrypting only a few columns misses data that leaks through other paths. Expect a small read/write performance penalty.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to persist a session token on Android?
options: EncryptedSharedPreferences backed by the Android Keystore
Plain SharedPreferences so the value is easy to read and update
A plain file under the app’s external storage directory
Keep it in memory only and force re-authentication at every process start
questions.explanation: EncryptedSharedPreferences plus the Keystore keeps the token confidential at rest. Plain SharedPreferences or plain files are extractable, and in-memory-only storage forces users to re-authenticate constantly. Always clear tokens (and any refresh logic) on logout.

questions.question: A user rotates the device, then Android kills your process. Where should you restore UI state that must survive process death?
options: A ViewModel holding state through SavedStateHandle
A static field in the Application class
An object reference stored in a companion object
A field on the Activity that is never cleared
questions.explanation: ViewModel + SavedStateHandle survive both configuration changes and process death. Static/Application fields and Activity fields die with the process and recreate awkwardly. Use onSaveInstanceState or rememberSaveable for small, parcelable transient state.

questions.question: Which modern, reliable Android API tells you which app is currently in the foreground?
options: UsageStatsManager query with the PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS permission
ActivityManager.getRunningTasks
PackageManager.queryIntentActivities
TelephonyManager.getCellLocation
questions.explanation: getRunningTasks has been restricted for third-party apps since Android 5.0; the sanctioned path is a UsageStatsManager query (or an accessibility service). These APIs exist with privacy guardrails, so be sure the use is legitimate.

questions.question: Which pipeline best represents a solid CI/CD setup for Android?
options: Build with Gradle caching, run unit/instrumented tests, lint, scan dependencies, then deploy to an internal track
Lint once, build release, and push straight to production
Run unit tests only and skip lint and security scanning
Hand-build APKs on a developer laptop and upload them manually
questions.explanation: A robust pipeline gates quality early: Gradle caching speeds builds, tests/lint give fast feedback, dependency scanning catches supply-chain risk, and an internal track gives a safe deployment target before production.

questions.question: Which set of practices best describes building an accessible Android app?
options: Content descriptions, 48dp touch targets, WCAG color contrast, large-text support, and TalkBack testing
Using larger fonts and nothing else
Focusing on color contrast alone
Replacing all touch UI with hardware buttons so the screen reader is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Accessibility is multi-faceted: labels for screen readers, adequate touch targets (48dp), sufficient contrast, support for text scaling, and validating with TalkBack/Accessibility Scanner. Addressing only one dimension leaves most users out.

questions.question: What is the idiomatic first step to make an Android app localizable?
options: Move all user-visible strings into strings.xml resources
Hardcode English text and branch on Locale.getDefault() in code
Bundle locale-specific text in a JSON config loaded at startup
Use strings.xml only for the app name and keep UI text hardcoded
questions.explanation: The Android resource system resolves string resources automatically per locale (values-* directories), which makes translation and RTL testing straightforward. Hardcoded strings cannot be localized, and hand-rolled configs duplicate what the framework provides.

questions.question: Which combination most directly improves network performance in an Android app?
options: OkHttp cache with HTTP cache headers, compression, pagination, and connection reuse
Opening more parallel threads to send more requests at once
Increasing the request timeout on every call
Switching every request to plain HTTP to remove TLS overhead
